reference.source: Volpe's Neurology of the Newborn / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A ciliopathy defined neuroradiologically by the molar tooth sign, produced by cerebellar vermis hypoplasia or aplasia together with thickened, horizontally oriented and elongated superior cerebellar peduncles and a deepened interpeduncular fossa

Classic neonatal picture combines episodic tachypnoea alternating with apnoea, abnormal eye movements including oculomotor apraxia and nystagmus, hypotonia evolving into ataxia, and developmental delay
Inheritance is usually autosomal recessive with marked genetic heterogeneity; more than thirty causative genes encode proteins of the primary cilium and basal body
Because it is a ciliopathy, extra-neurological involvement is common and defines subtypes, including retinal dystrophy, nephronophthisis or cystic renal disease, hepatic fibrosis, and polydactyly
The CEP290 and NPHP1 genotypes carry higher risk of renal disease, while TMEM67 is associated with hepatic fibrosis, guiding organ-directed surveillance
Cognitive outcome is variable and many children have moderate impairment, so early developmental support and multidisciplinary follow-up are important
Prenatal suspicion may arise from vermian abnormality on foetal imaging, and diagnosis is confirmed by the molar tooth sign on postnatal MRI plus molecular testing
reference.pathophysiology: Joubert syndrome is a disorder of the primary cilium and basal body (a ciliopathy). Pathogenic variants in genes encoding ciliary transition-zone and axonemal proteins disrupt ciliary signalling that guides mid-hindbrain patterning and axonal decussation. The resulting failure of cerebellar vermis development and abnormal crossing of superior cerebellar peduncle and corticospinal fibres produce the characteristic mid-hindbrain malformation seen as the molar tooth sign. The same ciliary dysfunction in the retina, renal tubule, and biliary tract accounts for the frequently associated multi-organ features.
additionalDifferentials: Dandy-Walker malformation and other posterior fossa cystic malformations
Cerebellar vermis hypoplasia from other causes such as congenital disorders of glycosylation
Other ciliopathies such as Meckel-Gruber and Bardet-Biedl syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to demonstrate the molar tooth sign and characterise vermian and brainstem anatomy
Molecular genetic testing, typically a ciliopathy gene panel or exome sequencing
Renal ultrasound and renal function testing to screen for nephronophthisis or cystic disease
Ophthalmological assessment with electroretinography for retinal dystrophy and oculomotor evaluation
Liver ultrasound and liver function tests to detect hepatic fibrosis
Developmental and neuropsychological assessment to guide support
redFlags: Neonatal apnoea and irregular breathing requiring respiratory monitoring
Progressive renal impairment from nephronophthisis leading to end-stage kidney disease
Signs of portal hypertension or hepatic decompensation from fibrosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the degree of neurological impairment and the extent of renal, hepatic, and retinal involvement. Many individuals survive into adulthood with variable cognitive and motor disability, but progressive kidney or liver disease can substantially affect life expectancy.
pitfalls: Attributing neonatal apnoea and hypotonia to birth asphyxia and missing the underlying malformation
Failing to recognise the molar tooth sign on suboptimal or non-dedicated posterior fossa imaging
Not screening for renal, hepatic, and retinal disease that may present years after the neurological diagnosis
Assuming a uniform prognosis despite wide genotype and phenotype variability
